item.title: Show HN: Self University - learn system engineering via interactive puzzles (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description:
I'm 18, I've solved 823 problems on LeetCode with a 430+ day streak, and I can tell you, it's a dry platform for solving algorithmic little tasks, and it has nothing to do with education. I am not saying it is bad, LeetCode is actually awesome, but it just does not teach you anything. I came here to fix this exact problem.

When you want to solve a new problem, you often run into the fact that you're seeing it for the first time, especially the topics that are in there. And then going off to read lectures or articles is not ideal, because you need to solve the problem here and now (otherwise it'd be constant context switching), not waste a ton of time on it, especially on those complicated problem statements.

All of the above can be applied to a lot of things in general, like reading docs, articles, AI slop, and other materials. The deal is simple: you find some info, read it, take notes, then you never come back to them (because it's long and boring to reread), and you forget it all.

So I started fixing all of these problems - convenient, fast, always at hand, and it's selfuniversity

https://selfuniversity.site

item.title: A ship fired a distress flare as fireworks. A ship went: This is our Christmas (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description:
I'm a navigation officer on commercial ships, seven years at sea. Two things here that might interest you.

First, promotion in the merchant service runs almost entirely on competency. Self-marketing, like a perfect CV, barely helps. Competency, like taking action during man overboard, mattered far more.

Second: on Christmas night, a ship fired a rocket parachute flare. Hundreds of ships saw it. That's a distress signal. Every vessel that sees one is obligated to report it. The radio played Christmas carols instead.

-

11pm. I was standing watch when I heard footsteps behind the curtains. A tall, broad-shouldered silhouette came out. Captain T. The sea was empty, and he had come up simply to look at it.

He told me about a competition with his dear friend who, alongside him, took to the sea. Same age, but his friend was the academy's honor student, Captain T. second by 0.02 CGPA. Graduating, they each bet $10,000 on who would first reach Captaincy.

His friend became an oil tanker Captain at 29, commanding some 100,000 GT. Captain T. attained his at 30, on gas tankers of the same capacity. Promotion is slower on larger carriers, and gas tankers carry the most stringent safety laws in the industry.

Still, he admitted, he had lost. His rival had secured recommendation letters from all Masters he sailed with. Praiseworthy, remarked Captain T.

29, and 30. I've sailed with Chief Officers ten years older, still struggling for promotion.

"Seafaring is straightforward work. There's really only one thing that truly mattered in gaining promotion: be as competent as you can be."

I once applied to other shipping companies. I spent weeks tinkering with my CV, optimizing it until it was two pages, structurally readable, credible. No reply.

A colleague had gotten into one of the highest paying companies in the world. I asked for his CV. Surely his was better than mine. Five pages, a grainy face picture, tangled sentences that read like a direct google translation. Poorly written, yet his employment took a month.

One difference: he applied when the company heavily advertised vacancies. They desperately needed people to man their newbuilt ships. Recruiters screened CVs only to short-list. The real judgment happened in the interview.

What mattered was one thing: how well could you perform your work. What's your action during a man overboard? Where do you divert when there's a fatal case for the crew? What's the safest way to board a ship? Seafaring is a vocation where self-marketing serves very little.

Sign-off dates aren't something to be planned. One would try, depending on the reliever's availability, but more often than not things would not go as planned. Christmas is the one you lose most.

Seamen found their own ways of celebrating missed moments. This event, I withhold its whereabouts and its year. What transpired was true.

Midnight 25th December. I was about to go down from the Bridge when I saw fireworks spring forth along the coasts. The VHF, tuned to Channel 16, usually busy with ships calling in positions, now played Christmas carols. It is a violation to use Channel 16 for anything but emergency traffic, but such breaches were untraceable when hundreds of ships cheered at once.

Even more illegal was what ensued minutes after. A bright red smoke shot to the sky. A rocket parachute flare, from one of the anchored ships. Pyrotechnics signal vessels in distress, and every ship seeing it must relay the message to the coast station, and potentially deviate course to rescue her. More than a violation, this broke international maritime law.

Following the flare were cheers on the radio by tens of ships. One voice has stayed with me since:

"This is our Christmas!"

The VHF turned more wildly than ever, the flare fired like an ordinary firecracker.

More essays: thenautology.substack.com

item.title: Gemini API removes postpay billing (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description:
Mail received:

We are writing to inform you of an upcoming billing change to Google AI Studio and the Gemini API.

We require developers to switch your Gemini API billing from Postpay to Prepay by September 14, 2026. This is part of our ongoing effort to improve our platform to give developers more control over API consumption and costs.

This change applies exclusively to your Gemini API usage in AI Studio. All other GCP services on your account will remain on Postpay. What you need to know

Key changes: Starting September 14, 2026, to use paid features in the Gemini API you will be required to change the billing plan associated with your Google AI Studio projects to Prepay. Learn more about the Prepay billing plan here.

item.title: Launch HN: Bullet (YC S26) - A Faster Coding Agent (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description:
Hi HN! We're Adi and Alex, founders of Bullet, a faster coding agent.

Bullet started in a senior year dorm room at Yale. We were fresh out of working at AppLovin and Citadel, so naturally, we just knew we were going to be startup gods. We were going to use our skills optimizing stock pricing calculation speeds and agent document context to take over the world.

Lo-and-behold, that year, Bullet was an AI hedge fund, a browser-use agent, synthetic financial data (oof), a mobile IDE, and a bunch of other things. We wanted to build something people wanted, but it seemed like everything we built was just terrible, useless, or both.

So, we decided to do something completely different, something completely out of the blue, something that no one had ever done before. Solve a problem we actually had.

Over the course of six pivots, we suffered. Throughout all of our adventures, one final boss kept getting in our way. Claude Code and his little brother Codex. We were spending hours waiting for coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, and got so frustrated to the point that I downloaded the Claude Code whip. We had spent months of time waiting for six codebases-worth of useless coding agent work.

Lightbulb moment. There's nothing more noble than destroying the institutions! Let's take on Claude Code and Codex, we can do it! Piece of cake!

And so, Bullet started off as a side project. We used the Claude Code to improve the Claude Code:

1. Model routing. Do you regret giving a task to Fable when it could have literally been done by Sonnet?

2. Targeted code + context search. We think embedding the whole repo is dumb. We also think sticking the whole context (or compressed context) in chat is dumb. So we do faster and better greps over both.

3. Aggressive context hygiene. Tool output is bounded, stale screenshots disappear, we don't re-read files...the garbage never floods the model.

4. Efficient turns. Batch independent investigation, make one surgical edit, then perform one focused verification. Internal measurement showed 16% fewer round trips and 27% lower cost.

5. The Flash. We prayed to Barry Allen for speed.

And thank the Flash, he gave us speed! On SWE-bench Verified, Bullet resolved 479/500 (95.8%) in one attempt, averaging 119s per task, 35-67% faster than mini-SWE-agent + Fable/Sol depending on task. Full results and methodology here (https://www.codewithbullet.com/blog/benchmark-results.html)

Eventually we started using it every day and never went back.

Listed above were just some of the things about Claude Code that frustrated us the most, but we are constantly optimizing every day (look at that, maybe we did learn something from our jobs).

So do you suffer? We are here for you. We understand.

Here's the video demo (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rWVmG5fRKgE)

Seriously speaking though, we hope that you guys try out Bullet if you are suffering with speed as much as we were, and we hope it brings you joy, rainbows, and faster responses. And if it's terrible, let us know it's terrible (we're masochists btw)! We'll be in the comments all day, you can also contact us at bullet@davidhf.com.

Thanks guys for listening to the larp :) try out codewithbullet.com. Again, that's codewithbullet.com. Again, that's codewi...

P.S: we hid a code on the website, see if you can unlock the secret page at the footer, all built with Bullet
